newsitem.title: CANADA: TimberWest says has expressions of interest.
newsitem.headline: TimberWest says has expressions of interest.

text.p: TimberWest Forest Ltd, which recently put itself up for sale, said Monday that it has received more than 20 expressions of interest.

"There have been expressions of interest," said chairman Doug Whitehead. "Twenty-odd groups," added chief executive Keith Purchase. They were speaking to reporters after the forest company's annual meeting.

Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd owns 52 percent of TimberWest. TimberWest was wholly owned by Fletcher until it was spun off in 1993. New Zealand's Fletcher Challenge Ltd owns a majority of Fletcher Canada.
The executives declined to identify or give the nationalities of the groups.
They said they were looking at all alternatives. Ideally they would like to retain the company's current structure but any decision to split it up would be up to the purchaser.
TimberWest expects the bidding process to take about three months and then another two to three months for the deal to gain approval from British Columbia's forest ministry.
TimberWest earlier Monday announced its first ever loss, but the company said it did not expect this to deter potential buyers.
Purchase said the company's strong cash flow in its first fiscal quarter of C$30.2 million was the second best in its history and a more important measure.
"I think most buyers look past the earnings to the underlying asset values," said Whitehead, referring to TimberWest's private forests and public timber licenses.
They declined to speculate whether the company would ultimately fetch more than its current share price of C$20.25.
The sale effort was prompted by Fletcher's decision to narrow its focus further on its paper business.
Whitehead, who is also president of Fletcher Canada, said Fletcher feels the "center of gravity of our assets is too heavily weighted" toward British Columbia.

But he said the decision to shed its stake in TimberWest did not mean it intends to abandon British Columbia, which has been criticized by forest executives for stricter regulations and new fees for the industry. "I don't think there is any room to grow here in B.C. in paper," he said.
While Fletcher wants to diversify its geography, Whitehead declined to say in response to a question whether it wanted to focus more heavily on the United States.

In the annual meeting, Purchase said TimberWest was in strong shape with a solid balance sheet and a strategic focus on selling wood products to the residential housing market in Japan and North America.

In the coming quarter, lumber prices are projected to be up 10 to 15 percent while in North America demand and prices for lumber "are even stronger than anticipated," he said. Housing starts have been boosted by low interest rates. In the British Columbia coastal market, pulp log prices are showing modest improvement and hemlock saw logs are expected to strengthen. The company is also seeking to improve returns from its coastal assets.
